title: The burning tail
hook: caught, set on fire, burns Lanka with it

segments.voice: Yesterday, finding Sita: a ring in, a jewel out. Your line was bring the ring. Who got your proof? Today, Hanuman could just go home. He doesn't. Day thirty-four.

The job is done. He's found Sita. He has her jewel. He could slip away tonight and nobody in Lanka would know he'd been there. But Hanuman wants to see the enemy up close. So he does something loud. He tears up the royal garden, tree by tree, until the guards come. He fights off one wave of warriors after another. Finally Ravana's son, Indrajit, binds him with a divine weapon, and Hanuman, who could break free, lets himself be tied up and dragged into the court of the ten-headed king. He wanted to be caught. It was the only way in the front door.
screen: `THE JOB IS DONE.` → `HE TEARS UP THE GARDEN.` → `HE LETS THEM CATCH HIM.`

segments.voice: Standing before Ravana, Hanuman speaks plainly. Give Sita back. Make peace with Rama. It's the wise thing. Ravana is furious and orders him killed. But his younger brother, Vibhishana, objects: you don't kill a messenger. That's not how kings behave. Remember Vibhishana; he matters later. So Ravana chooses a humiliation instead. A monkey's pride is his tail, he says. Burn it. The guards wrap Hanuman's tail in rags, soak it in oil, set it alight, and parade him through the streets to laughter. And then Hanuman shrinks, slips his ropes, grows huge again, and leaps up onto the rooftops. With his tail blazing, he jumps from palace to palace, and Lanka, the golden city, goes up in flames. They handed him the fire. He used it. The text adds something tender. When Sita hears they've set his tail on fire, she prays to Agni, the god of fire, that it be cool for him. And Hanuman notices, mid-leap, that the fire isn't hurting him at all. Then a sudden panic: what if I've burned the garden where she is? He rushes back. She's safe. The fire went everywhere except to her. Notice who picked the weapon. Ravana chose the fire, to make a fool of him. Hanuman turned it into a message. Sometimes what's handed to you, the setback, the insult, the thing meant to shrink you, turns out to be exactly the tool you needed. Use what they hand you.
screen: `GIVE HER BACK.` · `DON'T KILL A MESSENGER.` · `THEY SET THE TAIL ALIGHT.` · `SITA PRAYS: BE COOL FOR HIM.` · then, large: `USE WHAT THEY HAND YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a setback used. Sit and breathe. Think of something that was handed to you as a setback. A rejection. A criticism. A plan that fell through. Then ask: what did it make possible? What did you learn, or build, or find, because of it? If you can't see anything yet, that's fine. Just hold it and ask: what could this fire light? The bell holds the time.
Lanka, Ravana's island city, set ablaze when Hanuman turns his burning tail from a humiliation into fire across its rooftops, Sita's prayer keeping it cool for him.
Your line: use what they hand you. Today, take one thing that went wrong and ask what it's good for. Day thirty-four.

howItsDone: The burning of Lanka is a favorite scene in Ramlila performances across North India, and devotees recite it as part of the Sundara Kanda.

he lets himself be taken, to get into Ravana's court.

fork.setup: you're Hanuman. your tail is on fire and the whole city is laughing at you. what do you do?
options: beg Ravana to put it out.
slip the ropes and carry the fire across the rooftops.
run straight to the sea and escape.
fork.reveal: he leaps from palace to palace and Lanka burns. then he rushes back to make sure Sita is safe. she is.

original.note: Sanskrit: the island city of Ravana in the Ramayana.

trapdoor: what you thought: a monkey sets a city on fire.
what it means: the fire meant as a humiliation becomes his message, and Sita's prayer keeps it from hurting him.
what a scholar hears: in Valmiki, Hanuman's worry that he has burned Sita, and his relief, shows the poet's care; Vibhishana's objection foreshadows his later choice.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda 41–55 (the garden destroyed; Hanuman before Ravana; the tail; Lanka burns; Sita's prayer)

notes: Hanuman lets himself be bound by Indrajit's Brahma weapon out of respect for Brahma and to reach Ravana; simplified to 'lets himself be tied up'. Confirm.
Sita's prayer to Agni to be cool for Hanuman: Sundara Kanda ~53. Confirm.
Ravana's remark that a monkey's tail is his pride: follows Valmiki; confirm.
Audit (wider sample): replaced the stock turn 'Here's what the story knows', shared with most camp-2 scripts including days 33 and 35, with 'Notice who picked the weapon'.
